questions.q: Why can `doctest` test `pricing_core.hpp` without building the pybind11 extension at all?
options: doctest secretly compiles a hidden Python interpreter
The pricing core never includes any pybind11 header, so it is ordinary C++ that can be compiled and tested completely independently of Python
doctest can only test functions that return integers
pytest and doctest are actually the same tool under different names
questions.explain: Because the pricing core has no dependency on pybind11 or Python, a C++-only test framework like doctest can exercise it directly, with no compiled extension or Python interpreter involved.

questions.q: What does `pytest` verify in this capstone that a pure-C++ `doctest` suite cannot?
options: Nothing — the two test suites are completely redundant
The behavior of the actual pybind11 bindings and Python-facing API, including argument handling and the real import path a user goes through
Whether the C++ compiler is installed correctly
Whether the CMake version is new enough
questions.explain: pytest exercises the compiled extension as a real Python user would — importing it, passing NumPy arrays, and using keyword arguments — which a C++-only test of the pricing core cannot cover.

questions.q: Why does the benchmarking script implement `black_scholes_python` as a separate pure-Python function instead of just timing `qp.price_european` against itself?
options: Because qp.price_european cannot be timed with timeit
To establish a fair, honest baseline — the actual speedup claim requires comparing against an equivalent pure-Python implementation, not against nothing
Because pure Python functions run faster than compiled C++ by default
timeit requires at least two different functions to run at all
questions.explain: A speedup number is only meaningful relative to a real baseline. The pure-Python Black-Scholes implementation gives an honest point of comparison for the vectorized C++ path.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is a reviewer really assessing when they ask a candidate to "walk me through a project"?
options: Whether the candidate memorized the exact syntax of every library used
Whether the candidate can explain the trade-offs and decisions behind the project, not just list the technologies involved
Whether the project uses the newest possible C++ standard
Whether the project has the largest possible number of files
questions.explain: The lesson frames portfolio presentation around explaining decisions — architecture choices, concurrency design, measured results, and scope trade-offs — rather than simply naming technologies used.

questions.q: Why is `bond.price(0.05)` expected to equal approximately `1000.0` (the face value) for a `Bond(1000.0, 0.05, 10)` in the doctest suite?
options: Because all bonds are priced at exactly their face value regardless of inputs
Because a bond prices at par (equal to face value) precisely when the discount yield equals its coupon rate — a known identity used here as a sanity check
Because the Bond class always returns the face value due to a bug
Because 0.05 is an invalid yield and the function returns a default value
questions.explain: This is a standard bond-pricing identity: when the yield used for discounting equals the bond's coupon rate, the discounted cash flows sum exactly to the face value, making it a convenient test that needs no external reference table.
